claim: The Multi-Stage Model of Carcinogenesis (MMC) was developed in the 1950s-70s.
source: The Multi-Stage Model of Carcinogenesis (MMC), developed in the 1950 s-70s, postulated carcinogenesis as a Darwinian somatic selection process.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a historical fact.

claim: The MMC postulated carcinogenesis as a Darwinian somatic selection process.
source: The Multi-Stage Model of Carcinogenesis (MMC), developed in the 1950 s-70s, postulated carcinogenesis as a Darwinian somatic selection process.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of the MMC.

claim: The cellular organization of tissues was poorly understood when the MMC was developed.
source: The cellular organization of tissues was then poorly understood, with almost nothing known about cancer drivers and stem cells.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as historical context.

claim: Almost nothing was known about cancer drivers and stem cells when the MMC was developed.
source: The cellular organization of tissues was then poorly understood, with almost nothing known about cancer drivers and stem cells.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as historical context.

claim: The MMC paradigm was later confirmed.
source: The MMC paradigm was later confirmed, and cancer incidence was explained as a function of mutation occurrence.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a historical development.

claim: Cancer incidence was explained as a function of mutation occurrence.
source: The MMC paradigm was later confirmed, and cancer incidence was explained as a function of mutation occurrence.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a historical development.

claim: The MMC has never been tested for its ability to account for discrepancies in the number of driver mutations and stem cell compartment organization underlying different cancers that demonstrate nearly universal age-dependent incidence patterns.
source: However, the MMC has never been tested for its ability to account for the discrepancies in the number of driver mutations and the organization of the stem cell compartments underlying different cancers that still demonstrate nearly universal age-dependent incidence patterns.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a gap in the literature.

claim: Two additional major mechanisms need to be incorporated into the MMC to make it capable of generalizing cancer incidence across tissues and species: aging-dependent somatic selection and life history-dependent evolution of species-specific tumor suppressor mechanisms.
source: Here we demonstrate by Monte Carlo modeling the impact of key somatic evolutionary parameters on the MMC performance, revealing that two additional major mechanisms, aging-dependent somatic selection and life history-dependent evolution of species-specific tumor suppressor mechanisms, need to be incorporated into the MMC to make it capable of generalizing cancer incidence across tissues and species.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by the Monte Carlo modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fisher and Hollomon observed that the age distribution of cancer death rates follows the sixth power of age.
source: The theoretical foundations of the modern MMC originate from early observations by Fisher and Hollomon (Fisher and Hollomon, 1951) and Nordling (Nordling, 1953) that the age distribution of cancer death rates follows the sixth power of age.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with a citation to the original work.

claim: Nordling formulated the theory that cancer develops as a sequence of mutations that transform normal cells into malignant cells.
source: Nordling (Nordling, 1953) then formulated the theory and postulated that cancer develops as a sequence of mutations that transform normal cells into malignant cells.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with a citation to Nordling's work.

claim: Armitage and Doll proposed a mathematical model to substantiate the theory that cancer develops as a sequence of mutations.
source: Later, Armitage and Doll (Armitage and Doll, 1954) supported this idea and proposed a mathematical model to substantiate it.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with a citation to Armitage and Doll's work.

claim: Armitage and Doll's model required that the rate of mutation accumulation is the same throughout lifespan.
source: Armitage and Doll's model, as they acknowledged, also required that the rate of mutation accumulation is the same throughout lifespan, which was a reasonable assumption at the time.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a description of the original model's assumptions.

claim: Approximately 50% of mutations accumulate before maturity.
source: Multiple studies have later challenged this assumption, showing that ~50% of mutations accumulate before maturity (Dollé et al., 2000; Finette et al., 1994; Giese et al., 2002; Horvath, 2013), although this early life pattern of mutation accumulation is not universally observed (Welch et al., 2012; Blokzijl et al., 2016; Osorio et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with citations to multiple studies.

claim: The early life pattern of mutation accumulation is not universally observed.
source: Multiple studies have later challenged this assumption, showing that ~50% of mutations accumulate before maturity (Dollé et al., 2000; Finette et al., 1994; Giese et al., 2002; Horvath, 2013), although this early life pattern of mutation accumulation is not universally observed (Welch et al., 2012; Blokzijl et al., 2016; Osorio et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with citations to studies showing different patterns.

claim: The deceleration of mutation accumulation is explained by the considerable slowdown of stem cell division rate upon maturation.
source: The subsequent deceleration of mutation accumulation is now explained by the considerable slowdown of stem cell division rate upon maturation (Bowie et al., 2006; DeGregori, 2013; Rozhok and DeGregori, 2015; Sidorov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with citations to supporting studies.

claim: Armitage and Doll assumed a process driven by approximately six sequentially acquired mutations based on cancer incidence increasing as the sixth power of age.
source: Armitage and Doll therefore assumed a process driven by approximately six sequentially acquired mutations, based on cancer incidence increasing as the sixth power of age, and mentioned that many cancers behave analogously, with a supposedly similar underlying process of carcinogenesis.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a description of Armitage and Doll's reasoning.

claim: Cancers are driven by very different mutations and require very different numbers of drivers, yet show very similar temporal distribution with age.
source: Further research, however, demonstrated that cancers are driven by very different mutations and require very different numbers of drivers, and yet these cancers still show very similar temporal distribution with age.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a key observation that challenges the MMC.

claim: Peter Nowell developed the concept of clonal selection during carcinogenesis.
source: Later, the theory was solidified by Peter Nowell who developed the concept of clonal selection during carcinogenesis (Nowell, 1976) and put the model within its current general framework.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with a citation to Nowell's work.

claim: Childhood cancers drastically deviate from the observed age-dependent pattern and are difficult to explain.
source: Some fundamental problems, however, were already noticed by early theorists, when Fisher and Hollomon mentioned that childhood cancers drastically deviate from the observed age-dependent pattern and are difficult to explain (Fisher and Hollomon, 1951).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with a citation to Fisher and Hollomon.

claim: Different cancers originate from very different stem cell systems with different lifetime stem cell numbers and cell division profiles.
source: An additional complication that early theorists were unaware of is the fact that different cancers originate from very different stem cell systems, with different lifetime stem cell numbers and cell division profiles.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a complication for the MMC.

claim: More recent models of age-dependent cancer incidence operate with the stem/progenitor cell paradigm of cancer origins.
source: More recent models of age-dependent cancer incidence do operate with the stem/progenitor cell paradigm of cancer origins (Calabrese and Shibata, 2010; Gerstung and Beerenwinkel, 2010; Michor et al., 2004; Beerenwinkel et al., 2007; McFarland et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with citations to recent modeling studies.

claim: Analytical models used so far have not been tested for their ability to explain age-dependent incidence for cancers driven by different numbers of mutations and originating in stem cell pools of varying sizes.
source: However, the analytical models used so far have not been tested for their ability to explain age-dependent incidence for cancers driven by different numbers of mutations and originating in stem cell pools of varying sizes.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a gap in the literature.

claim: Models comparing and unifying the principles of cancer progression of multiple cancer types and across multiple species are lacking.
source: Models comparing and unifying the principles of cancer progression of multiple cancer types and across multiple species are lacking.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a gap in the literature.

claim: The current MMC lacks consideration of fundamental evolutionary processes shaping the evolution of animal life history traits.
source: Critically, the current MMC lacks consideration of fundamental evolutionary processes shaping the evolution of animal life history traits (such as longevity, body size, and reproductive strategies) and, as such and despite multiple claims otherwise, has so far not been placed within the framework of evolutionary theory.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a criticism of the current MMC.

claim: Most cancers have very similar temporal incidence dynamics, demonstrating approximately the same fractional increases in incidence with age.
source: While different cancers vary significantly in lifetime risk and total incidence, most cancers have very similar temporal incidence dynamics, demonstrating approximately the same fractional increases in incidence with age.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a key observation.

claim: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) in chronic phase is driven by one mutation.
source: Cancers driven by one mutation, such as chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) in chronic phase, exhibit age-dependent kinetics of incidence that are quite similar to cancers that require many more mutations, including leukemias like acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and chronic lymphoblastic leukemia (CLL) thought to also originate in hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) pools and colon cancers which originate in highly fragmented stem cell pools (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as an example of a single-mutation cancer.

claim: CML exhibits age-dependent kinetics of incidence that are quite similar to cancers that require many more mutations.
source: Cancers driven by one mutation, such as chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) in chronic phase, exhibit age-dependent kinetics of incidence that are quite similar to cancers that require many more mutations, including leukemias like acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and chronic lymphoblastic leukemia (CLL) thought to also originate in hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) pools and colon cancers which originate in highly fragmented stem cell pools (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction and supported by Figure 1A-C showing similar incidence patterns.

claim: AML and CLL are thought to originate in hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) pools.
source: Cancers driven by one mutation, such as chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) in chronic phase, exhibit age-dependent kinetics of incidence that are quite similar to cancers that require many more mutations, including leukemias like acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and chronic lymphoblastic leukemia (CLL) thought to also originate in hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) pools and colon cancers which originate in highly fragmented stem cell pools (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a description of the origin of these cancers.

claim: Colon cancers originate in highly fragmented stem cell pools.
source: Cancers driven by one mutation, such as chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) in chronic phase, exhibit age-dependent kinetics of incidence that are quite similar to cancers that require many more mutations, including leukemias like acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and chronic lymphoblastic leukemia (CLL) thought to also originate in hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) pools and colon cancers which originate in highly fragmented stem cell pools (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a description of the origin of colon cancers.

claim: Hematopoietic clones driven by a single driver mutation increase with age, following a very similar incidence increase as mutationally more complex cancers.
source: Moreover, hematopoietic clones driven by a single driver mutation, also thought to originate in HSC pools, have also been shown to increase with age, following a very similar incidence increase as mutationally more complex cancers (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction and supported by Figure 1D showing clonal hematopoiesis data.

claim: Cancer incidence closely follows the physiological aging curve in animals.
source: As in humans, cancer incidence closely follows the physiological aging curve in other animals (Albuquerque et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with a citation to Albuquerque et al., 2018.

claim: Cancer incidence scales to lifespan, but not to body size.
source: Incidence thus scales to lifespan, but not to body size, a problem demonstrating significant deviations of cancer incidence from cell numbers and known as Peto's paradox (Peto et al., 1975).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with a citation to Peto et al., 1975.

claim: Somatic selection in tissues depends on tissue microenvironment.
source: Somatic selection in tissues, just like selection in populations, depends on tissue microenvironment.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a theoretical proposition.

claim: The long co-evolution of stem cells and tissue regulatory processes should have adapted stem cells to the well-regulated microenvironments of a fit body.
source: The long co-evolution of stem cells and tissue regulatory processes should have adapted stem cells to the well-regulated microenvironments of a fit body, which should make the normal cells highly fit and should promote stabilizing selection and purifying selection against most phenotype-altering mutations.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a theoretical proposition based on evolutionary principles.

claim: Aging disrupts tissue ecosystems and should promote positive selection for random mutants, including oncogenic mutations, that are adaptive to the new microenvironments.
source: Aging disrupts tissue ecosystems, and like environmental change for organismal populations, should promote positive selection for random mutants, including oncogenic mutations, that are adaptive to the new microenvironments.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a theoretical proposition.

claim: The character of age-dependent clonal evolution and clonal expansions is tightly linked with age-dependent cancer incidence.
source: We assume in this study that the character of age-dependent clonal evolution and clonal expansions is tightly linked with age-dependent cancer incidence, which has been shown for the hematopoietic system (McKerrell et al., 2015; Genovese et al., 2014; Jaiswal et al., 2014; Xie et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as an assumption of the study, supported by citations to studies on the hematopoietic system.

claim: The MMC model holds generally and is robust against departures from mutation accumulation linearity required by the original Armitage-Doll model.
source: Our results demonstrate that the MMC model holds generally and is robust against departures from mutation accumulation linearity required by the original Armitage-Doll model.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a result of the study.

claim: The MMC reproduces the general exponential shape of cancer incidence and clonal dynamics regardless of whether stem cell divisions remain stable or change dramatically during body maturation.
source: The MMC thus reproduces the general exponential shape of cancer incidence and clonal dynamics regardless of whether stem cell divisions remain stable or change dramatically during body maturation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a result of the study.

claim: Differences in the required number of driver mutations, mutation rate and driver strength cause the MMC to fail to reproduce the expected temporal correlation in the incidence of different cancers.
source: However, differences in the required number of driver mutations, mutation rate and driver strength cause the MMC to fail to reproduce the expected temporal correlation in the incidence of different cancers.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a result of the study.

claim: The current MMC is incapable of explaining the incidence of childhood leukemia.
source: The current MMC is also incapable of explaining the incidence of childhood leukemia.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a result of the study.

claim: Differential aging-dependent somatic selection improves the performance of the MMC and partially resolves problems with explaining cancer incidence patterns.
source: We demonstrate that differential aging-dependent somatic selection improves the performance of the MMC and partially resolves these problems.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a result of the study.

claim: The model operates with a simulated pool of cells of varying dynamic or stable sizes competing for niche space as one effective population.
source: Our model operates with a simulated pool of cells of varying dynamic or stable sizes competing for niche space as one effective population.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Quick guide to model section as a description of the model design.

claim: The model design most closely replicates clonal processes in the human HSC system of the bone marrow.
source: This design most closely replicates clonal processes in the human HSC system of the bone marrow.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Quick guide to model section as a description of the model design.

claim: HSCs are effectively one population of cells that divide, differentiate and compete for a limited bone marrow niche space.
source: Multiple studies demonstrate that HSCs are effectively one population of cells that divide, differentiate and compete for a limited bone marrow niche space (Abkowitz et al., 1996; Abkowitz et al., 2000; Catlin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Quick guide to model section with citations to supporting studies.

claim: HSCs have a well-established proclivity to migrate.
source: Their spatial segregation in different bones is compensated by the HSC's well-established proclivity to migrate (Wright et al., 2001), making their competition to a large extent uniform across the body over time.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Quick guide to model section with a citation to Wright et al., 2001.

claim: Most leukemias are believed to initiate in the HSC compartment.
source: HSCs represent a good population for modeling somatic evolution, as most leukemias are believed to initiate in the HSC compartment (Fialkow et al., 1967; Jan et al., 2012; Kikushige et al., 2011; Miyamoto et al., 2000; Shlush et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Quick guide to model section with citations to supporting studies.

claim: The size of the simulated SC pool increases early in life and reaches its adult size by 18–20 years of age.
source: The size of the simulated SC pool increases early in life and reaches its adult size by 18–20 years of age (Figure 2B upper chart).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Quick guide to model section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cell division rates change in an age-dependent manner during body growth and maturation.
source: Cell division rates change in a similar age-dependent manner (Figure 2B lower chart) during body growth and maturation (Bowie et al., 2006; Sidorov et al., 2009), or division rates are kept stable (for experimental purposes).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Quick guide to model section with citations and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Non-linear changes in cell division rates early in life do not have a significant influence on the model's capability to replicate an exponential succession of clones driven by accumulating a series of driver mutations.
source: The results shown in Figure 3A demonstrate that non-linear changes in cell division rates early in life do not have a significant influence on the model's capability to replicate an exponential succession of clones driven by accumulating a series of driver mutations.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 3A showing simulation results.

claim: Clones with different numbers of drivers have different timing of expansions.
source: Figure 3A also shows that clones with different numbers of drivers have different timing of expansions.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Even with rapidly decelerating stem cell division rates causing early accumulation of mutations, under select assumptions for numbers of required driver mutations and mutation rate, the current MMC model is still capable of replicating higher late-life rates of somatic evolution.
source: We can therefore conclude that even with rapidly decelerating stem cell division rates causing early accumulation of mutations, under select assumptions for numbers of required driver mutations and mutation rate, the current MMC model is still capable of replicating higher late-life rates of somatic evolution, perhaps due to the waiting time necessary for initiated cells to expand into larger clones.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: MMC-DS can reproduce late-life increases in somatic evolution rates due to the stronger late-life positive selection.
source: MMC-DS also can reproduce late-life increases in somatic evolution rates due to the stronger late-life positive selection.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: The cell division profile does not discriminate between MMC-DS and the standard MMC.
source: The cell division profile, therefore, does not discriminate between MMC-DS and the standard MMC, suggesting that both models, so far, appear plausible.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: The effects of a range of adult cell division rates within the dynamic cell division profile is rather modest.
source: Figure 3B also shows that the effects of a range of adult cell division rates within the dynamic cell division profile is rather modest.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The MMC-DS model delays high rates of clonal evolution until the later portion of the simulated lifespan.
source: As with age-dependent cell division profiles, the noticeable difference is that the MMC-DS model delays high rates of clonal evolution until the later portion of the simulated lifespan.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an observation from the simulation results.

claim: Both MMC and MMC-DS are sensitive to mutation rate.
source: Expectedly, both MMC and MMC-DS are sensitive to mutation rate.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an observation from the simulation results.

claim: The MMC-DS model, unlike MMC, prevents all clones from expanding through youth (the period of likely reproduction).
source: The MMC-DS model, unlike MMC, prevents all clones from expanding through youth (the period of likely reproduction).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an observation from the simulation results.

claim: The number of drivers has much less of an effect within the MMC-DS model, with expansion kinetics delayed until and compressed in old age.
source: Still, the number of drivers has much less of an effect within the MMC-DS model, with expansion kinetics delayed until and compressed in old age.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an observation from the simulation results.

claim: A greater fitness advantage accelerates somatic evolution rates in both MMC and MMC-DS models.
source: As intuitively anticipated, a greater fitness advantage accelerates somatic evolution rates in both models (Figure 4A; red is the greatest fitness advantage).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: MMC-DS, unlike MMC, delays all clonal expansions until old age (independent of driver mutation numbers).
source: However, as with mutation rate, MMC-DS, unlike MMC, delays all clonal expansions until old age (independent of driver mutation numbers).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an observation from the simulation results.

claim: It is not necessary for early life selection acting on somatic mutants to be negative for MMC-DS to delay clonal expansions.
source: The MMC-DS(b) modeling (Figure 4A) demonstrates that it is not necessary for early life selection acting on somatic mutants to be negative. Even in the absence of negative selection (red lines, the early life fitness value is the same as for non-mutant cells), the age-dependent character of clonal expansions predicted by MMC-DS holds.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Increasing pool size does not increase the relative presence of mutant clones in it.
source: Figure 4B shows that the mentioned factors effectively counteract each other – increasing pool size does not increase the relative presence of mutant clones in it, and this relationship largely holds for both MMC and MMC-DS.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: MMC appears more sensitive to stem cell pool size than MMC-DS.
source: However, MMC appears more sensitive to stem cell pool size (which should increase for larger body size).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an observation from the simulation results.

claim: Earlier aging that produces earlier onset of positive selection on mutant cells leads to corresponding earlier expansions of mutant clones accumulating a series of driver mutations.
source: Figure 4C shows, as expected, that earlier aging that produces earlier onset of positive selection on mutant cells leads to corresponding earlier expansions of mutant clones accumulating a series of driver mutations.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Under the MMC-DS assumption of shifting selection, many clones demonstrate a minor peak very early in life, but are later suppressed until the second half of the simulated lifespan.
source: Figure 5B shows that under the MMC-DS assumption of shifting selection, many clones demonstrate a minor peak very early in life, but are later suppressed until the second half of the simulated lifespan.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The reason why very early clones are capable of forming small peaks is the larger presence of random drift imposed by the smaller pool size relative to the adult pool, interacting with faster cell division rates.
source: The reason why very early clones are capable of forming small peaks is the larger presence of random drift imposed by the smaller pool size relative to the adult pool, interacting with faster cell division rates (generating more mutations).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an explanation for the observed pattern.

claim: Clonal dynamics in HSC pools might provide an explanation for the elevated rates of leukemia in early childhood.
source: As we have previously shown (Rozhok et al., 2016), such clonal dynamics in HSC pools might provide an explanation for the elevated rates of leukemia in early childhood.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with a citation to previous work.

claim: Replication of the full pattern of leukemia incidence requires the MMC-DS model assumption of differential selection, whereby early portions of lifespan are characterized by a general suppression of somatic evolution by means of purifying selection.
source: However, these results show that replication of the full pattern of leukemia incidence requires the MMC-DS model assumption of differential selection, whereby early portions of lifespan are characterized by a general suppression of somatic evolution by means of purifying selection.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: The general principle of successive cell transformations proposed by Nordling, Armitage and Doll recapitulates the late-life exponential increases in the rates of somatic evolution regardless of the non-linear pre-maturity shifts in stem cell division rates.
source: Our results indicate that the general principle of successive cell transformations proposed by Nordling, Armitage and Doll (Nordling, 1953; Armitage and Doll, 1954) and later developed into the modern Multi-Stage Model of Carcinogenesis (MMC) recapitulates the late-life exponential increases in the rates of somatic evolution regardless of the non-linear pre-maturity shifts in stem cell division rates.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The MMC requires the incorporation of differential aging-dependent somatic selection acting on somatic cell variants in order to universally postpone increased rates of somatic evolution to late ages, independent of the number of driver mutations and the magnitude of the somatic selective value of these mutations.
source: The model, however, requires the incorporation of differential aging-dependent somatic selection acting on somatic cell variants, a principle earlier proposed as a key postulate of the Adaptive Oncogenesis model (DeGregori, 2011), in order to universally postpone increased rates of somatic evolution to late ages, independent of the number of driver mutations and the magnitude of the somatic selective value of these mutations.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The principle of aging-dependent somatic selection can potentially explain the scaling of increased cancer incidence to the species-specific lifespan.
source: This principle of aging-dependent somatic selection can potentially explain the scaling of increased cancer incidence to the species-specific lifespan, such that most cancers occur after 1.5 years for mice and 50 years for humans.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a theoretical proposition.

claim: The current MMC does not explain why most cancers show strikingly similar late life patterns of incidence, despite requiring very different numbers of driver mutations and originating in very different sized/organized stem cell pools.
source: The current MMC does not explain a very puzzling phenomenon – that most cancers show strikingly similar late life patterns of incidence, despite the fact that these cancers require very different numbers of driver mutations and originate in very different sized/organized stem cell pools (whether for different tissues or in different species).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a problem with the current MMC.

claim: Previous attempts to explain the age-dependence of multi-stage carcinogenesis have mostly used analytical modeling, with fixed effects of mutations on cellular fitness.
source: Previous attempts to explain the age-dependence of multi-stage carcinogenesis have mostly used analytical modeling, with fixed effects of mutations on cellular fitness (Calabrese and Shibata, 2010; Gerstung and Beerenwinkel, 2010; Michor et al., 2004; Beerenwinkel et al., 2007; McFarland et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: Fitness is a dynamic phenomenon that arises at the interface of phenotype and environment and is determined by the mode of selection acting on a phenotype.
source: However, fitness is a dynamic phenomenon that arises at the interface of phenotype and environment and is determined by the mode of selection acting on a phenotype, the latter being typically defined by environment (Wade and Kalisz, 1990).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with a citation to Wade and Kalisz, 1990.

claim: The MMC-DS model demonstrates early life increases in the rates of somatic evolution, mirroring the risk of early childhood cancers.
source: The MMC-DS model also demonstrates early life increases in the rates of somatic evolution, mirroring the risk of early childhood cancers, which does not arise from the standard MMC model.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a result of the study.

claim: Early-life processes should be driven by drift due to the small initial pool of stem cells in a fetus and right after birth.
source: As we have argued before (Rozhok et al., 2016), these early-life processes should be driven by drift due to the small initial pool of stem cells in a fetus and right after birth.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with a citation to previous work.

claim: Later suppression of somatic evolution until older ages can be explained by purifying somatic selection that acts in larger adult stem cell pools during reproductive periods of life-spans.
source: Later suppression of somatic evolution until older ages can be explained by purifying somatic selection that acts in larger adult stem cell pools during reproductive periods of life-spans.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a theoretical explanation.

claim: Early childhood cancers mostly comprise malignancies originating in large stem cell systems, such as hematopoietic.
source: Consistent with this logic, early childhood cancers mostly comprise malignancies originating in large stem cell systems, such as hematopoietic, while childhood carcinomas, which originate in the small fragmented epithelial stem cell compartments where drift dominates, are rare (www.seer.cancer.gov) (Rozhok et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with a citation to SEER data and previous work.

claim: Childhood carcinomas, which originate in the small fragmented epithelial stem cell compartments where drift dominates, are rare.
source: Consistent with this logic, early childhood cancers mostly comprise malignancies originating in large stem cell systems, such as hematopoietic, while childhood carcinomas, which originate in the small fragmented epithelial stem cell compartments where drift dominates, are rare (www.seer.cancer.gov) (Rozhok et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with a citation to SEER data and previous work.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated how the somatic fitness effects of oncogenic mutations can be dramatically affected by the age of the host.
source: Indeed, previous studies have demonstrated how the somatic fitness effects of oncogenic mutations can be dramatically affected by the age of the host (Henry et al., 2010; Henry et al., 2015; Parikh et al., 2018; Vas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citations to supporting studies.

claim: Somatic selection in the body and germline selection in a population are directly linked with mutual feedback acting on each other through reproductive success.
source: Based on the above presented results, we propose that somatic selection in the body and germline selection in a population are directly linked with mutual feedback acting on each other through reproductive success as shown in Figure 6.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a theoretical proposition and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Somatic selection impacts age-dependent tissue and individual fitness, and thus provides the fuel for germline selection operating on individual fitness.
source: Somatic selection, as the main determinant of somatic evolution in a tissue, impacts age-dependent tissue and individual fitness, and thus provides the fuel for germline selection operating on individual fitness.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a theoretical proposition.

claim: The effect of somatic mutations on cell somatic fitness is subject to germline selection based on an individual's fitness/health risks conferred by particular somatic mutations.
source: In this way, the effect of somatic mutations on cell somatic fitness is subject to germline selection based on an individual's fitness/health risks conferred by particular somatic mutations.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a theoretical proposition.

claim: Reproductive success provides a quantitative effect whereby the strength and directionality of germline selection acting on particular somatic cell alterations is determined by the overall reduction in reproductive success of an individual.
source: Reproductive success provides a quantitative effect whereby the strength and directionality of germline selection acting on particular somatic cell alterations is determined by the overall reduction in reproductive success of an individual.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a theoretical proposition.

claim: Germline selection acts on the effects of somatic mutations on cellular physiology depending on a species-specific general age-dependent mortality profile.
source: Therefore, germline selection acts on the effects of somatic mutations on cellular physiology depending on a species-specific general age-dependent mortality profile.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a theoretical proposition.

claim: Germline selection for tumor suppressive mechanisms is somatic mutation-specific and species-specific.
source: Such a model implies that germline selection for tumor suppressive mechanisms is somatic mutation-specific and species-specific.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a theoretical proposition.

claim: Aging-dependent differential selection regulated at the tissue level is likely a mechanism common across animal species.
source: Based on these principles and the mechanisms shown in Figure 6, we therefore argue that aging-dependent differential selection regulated at the tissue level and being likely a mechanism common across animal species should work in concert with additional inherited mechanisms of tumor suppression that are shaped by the evolution of life history traits of a particular species.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a theoretical proposition.

claim: Evidence of unique tumor suppression mechanisms already exists for multiple species.
source: Evidence of such unique mechanisms already exists for multiple species (Seluanov et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with a citation to Seluanov et al., 2018.

claim: A specific type of hyaluronic acid in the naked mole rat is believed to underlie the species' exceptional cancer protection capabilities.
source: A notable example is a specific type of hyaluronic acid in the naked mole rat that is believed to underlie the species' exceptional cancer protection capabilities (Tian et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with a citation to Tian et al., 2013.

claim: Alterations in p53 genes in elephants represent a potential group-specific mechanism to delay tumorigenesis till older ages.
source: Similarly, alterations in p53 genes in elephants represent a potential group-specific mechanism to delay tumorigenesis till older ages (Abegglen et al., 2015; Sulak et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citations to Abegglen et al., 2015 and Sulak et al., 2016.

claim: Tumor suppressive mechanisms tailored to limit the impact of classes of cancer driver mutations could be either species-specific or common across mammals or even animals.
source: Based on the principle shown in Figure 6, tumor suppressive mechanisms tailored to limit the impact of classes of cancer driver mutations (or particular pathways altered in cancers) could be either species-specific or common across mammals or even animals.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a theoretical proposition.

claim: The general aging-dependent shift in somatic selection and the evolved group-specific pathway-tailored tumor suppressor mechanisms can be viewed as essentially two different dimensions of which the overall mechanism regulating tumor suppression in animals is composed.
source: The general aging-dependent shift in somatic selection and the evolved group-specific pathway-tailored tumor suppressor mechanisms can be viewed as essentially two different dimensions of which the overall mechanism regulating tumor suppression in animals is composed.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a theoretical proposition.

claim: A number of cancers deviate from the general late-life pattern and occur at earlier ages, and these cancers tend to be associated with infections, to be very rare, and/or associated with modern lifestyles and conditions.
source: Alongside childhood cancers, a number of cancers deviate from the general late-life pattern and occur at earlier ages. These cancers tend to be associated with infections (e.g. Burkitt's lymphoma) (Grywalska and Rolinski, 2015), to be very rare (e.g. testicular cancers; www.seer.cancer.gov), and/or associated with modern lifestyles and conditions (e.g. breast cancer) (Layde et al., 1989; Hochberg and Noble, 2017; Giraudeau et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citations to supporting studies.

claim: Increased cancer incidence in humans and captive animals mirrors the species-specific aging profile and occurs after the ages most individuals of the species survive in the wild.
source: It is therefore not surprising that increased cancer incidence in humans and captive animals mirrors the species-specific aging profile and occurs after the ages most individuals of the species survive in the wild (Albuquerque et al., 2018), as both processes are shaped largely by the same germline selection forces.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with a citation to Albuquerque et al., 2018.

claim: Differential aging-dependent somatic selection in cooperation with the group-specific evolution of particular genes and cellular machinery that depends on the evolution of life history traits are sufficient to generalize the process of carcinogenesis.
source: We argue that differential aging-dependent somatic selection in cooperation with the group-specific evolution of particular genes, as well as cellular machinery in general, that depends on the evolution of life history traits are sufficient to generalize the process of carcinogenesis such that even phenomena such as early peaks in childhood cancer incidence of some cancers, Peto's paradox, and the universal lifespan-dependent pattern of cancer incidence can be explained within one theoretical paradigm that places the theory of somatic evolution within the framework of general evolutionary theory.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as the main theoretical conclusion of the study.

claim: The simulation starts with a small pool of 300 cells which grows by the simulated age of 18–20 years up to 10,000 cells.
source: The simulation starts with a small pool of 300 cells which grows by the simulated age of 18–20 years up to 10,000 cells, following estimates by Catlin et al. (2011) and Abkowitz et al. (2002).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section as a description of the model parameters.

claim: Estimates for the number of human HSCs range within ~10^4 to 3 × 10^5.
source: Estimates for the number of human HSCs range within ~104 to 3 × 105, however our model investigated relative clonal dynamics of somatic mutant under different assumptions, therefore the exact adult size of the simulated pool is not critically important.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section as background information.

claim: The simulation was updated each simulated 'week' and lasted through 5200 updates, simulating thus a lifespan of 100 years.
source: The simulation was updated each simulated 'week' (the basic model update step) and lasted through 5200 updates, simulating thus a lifespan of 100 years.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section as a description of the model parameters.

claim: The average simulated cell division rates started from ~1 division in 3 weeks and reached the adult rate of ~1 division in 40 weeks.
source: Following this paradigm, the average simulated cell division rates started from ~1 division in 3 weeks and reached the adult rate of ~1 division in 40 weeks (Catlin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section as a description of the model parameters.

claim: The phenotypic mutation rate is higher than typically expected mutation rates for DNA base pair substitutions, as it integrates all possible changes (including epigenetic) in a cell that can endow the cell with a significant heritable alteration in somatic fitness.
source: The phenotypic mutation rate is higher than typically expected mutation rates for DNA base pair substitutions, as it integrates all possible changes (including epigenetic) in a cell that can endow the cell with a significant heritable alteration in somatic fitness.

claim: The combined effect of multiple phenotype altering mutations is synergistic rather than additive.
